primary_sources: Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library & Museums, “Frequently Asked Questions on the 1876 Election”

stimulus.text:
| 1876 presidential election | Samuel J. Tilden (Democrat) | Rutherford B. Hayes (Republican) |
| Popular vote | 4,288,546 | 4,034,311 |
| Electoral votes, first count | 184 | 165 |

Twenty electoral votes were disputed: Florida (4), Louisiana (8), South Carolina (7), and one from Oregon. A candidate needed 185 electoral votes to win.
stimulus.source_note: Popular and electoral vote figures from the Rutherford B. Hayes Presidential Library & Museums, “Frequently Asked Questions on the 1876 Election.”

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table shows that the 1876 election was disputed mainly because

options.text: Hayes won the popular vote but lost the electoral vote.
options.misconception: The table shows Tilden ahead in the popular vote; Hayes lost it by about 250,000 votes.

options.text: neither candidate won a majority of the popular vote.
options.misconception: Background: Tilden won a majority of the popular vote, about 51 percent; the problem was the electoral count.

options.text: the House of Representatives had to choose the president.
options.misconception: Background: the House never chose; Congress created an Electoral Commission instead.

options.text: Tilden stood one electoral vote short, with 20 votes disputed.

rationales.A: The table shows Tilden ahead in the popular vote; Hayes lost it by about 250,000 votes.
rationales.B: Background: Tilden won a majority of the popular vote, about 51 percent; the problem was the electoral count.
rationales.C: Background: the House never chose; Congress created an Electoral Commission instead.
rationales.D: Tilden needed 185 electoral votes and held 184, while 20 more sat in dispute. One disputed state either way would decide the presidency, so both parties claimed the same votes.
rationales.general:
1. Read the popular vote row: Tilden leads by about 250,000 votes, so the popular result is clear.
2. Read the electoral row: Tilden has 184, one short of the 185 needed to win.
3. Read the note: 20 more electoral votes are disputed across four states.
4. With one vote short and twenty in doubt, the election had no lawful winner yet.
Remember: an election becomes a crisis when the rules give no winner and both sides can claim the same votes.
